The phrase “original sin” does not appear in Scripture. Not in Genesis. Not in Romans. Not in any epistle, gospel, or prophetic text in any canon — 66 books, 73, or 81.

The doctrine was systematized and given its definitive Western form by Augustine of Hippo in the late fourth century. Earlier writers, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Cyprian, had discussed Adam’s transgression and its effects on humanity. But the specific claim that guilt itself transmits biologically from Adam to every descendant was Augustine’s contribution. Before Augustine, no surviving Christian writer had developed inherited guilt into a systematic doctrine comparable to the form that would later dominate the Latin West.

What followed reshaped Western Christianity. Whether it recovered something already present in Paul’s letters or introduced something the text doesn’t require depends on which tradition you ask and which translation they’re reading.

That last part matters more than most people realize.

The Verse

Romans 5:12 is the load-bearing text. In Greek, Paul wrote:

“Because of this, just as sin entered into the world through one man, and death through sin, so also death passed to all men, because all sinned.” - “eph’ hō pantes hēmarton.”

That final phrase is where the fault line runs.

The Greek eph’ hō is a contraction of the preposition epi with a relative pronoun. Most modern scholars, across Catholic, Protestant, and Orthodox lines, translate it as “because.” Death spread to all men because all sinned.

But Augustine read Romans in Latin. The Old Latin versions used across the Western churches rendered eph’ hō as in quo — “in whom.” Death spread to all men in whom — that is, in Adam, all sinned.

The difference matters. “Because all sinned” means every person sins and therefore dies. It describes a pattern. “In whom all sinned” means every person was already implicated in Adam’s act before they drew breath. It describes an inheritance.

Both readings have had serious defenders. The Latin in quo carried Western theology for over a thousand years. The Greek eph’ hō is what Paul actually wrote. Most contemporary scholars, including many sympathetic to Augustinian theology, acknowledge the grammatical point while noting that Augustine’s broader case did not rest on this verse alone. He also cited Psalm 51:5, Job 14:4, Genesis 8:21, and John 3:3-5.

Romans 5:12 supplied Augustine’s strongest textual support for inherited guilt, though defenders have also appealed to Romans 5:18-19 and the Adam-Christ parallel more broadly.”l

The Case For

The doctrine of original sin draws on more than one verse, and its defenders have never lacked for scriptural ground.

Romans 5:12-19 is the fullest statement. Paul sets up a sustained parallel between Adam and Christ: “through one man’s offense judgment came to all men, resulting in condemnation” (v. 18), and “by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners” (v. 19). The logic is symmetrical, if Christ’s act of righteousness benefits all who are in him, then Adam’s act of disobedience implicates all who descend from him. The passage treats both figures as representative heads whose single acts carry consequences for everyone connected to them.

1 Corinthians 15:22 states the parallel in its starkest form: “For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all shall be made alive.” Defenders of original sin read this as confirming a real solidarity between Adam and all humanity, not merely that people imitate Adam’s sin, but that they are genuinely bound up in it.

Psalm 51:5: “Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin my mother conceived me,” has been read since Augustine as evidence that sinfulness precedes any conscious act. David traces his condition not to a choice he made, but to his very conception.

Genesis 8:21: “the imagination of man’s heart is evil from his youth,” and Ephesians 2:3: “we were by nature children of wrath,” round out a textual tradition that depicts the human condition as damaged at a level deeper than personal choice.

These texts are not marginal. They sit in Torah, Psalms, the Gospels, and the Pauline corpus. They have persuaded the majority of Western Christian theology for sixteen centuries. Whatever questions arise about Augustine’s specific formulation, the biblical material he built on is substantial.

The Case Against

Other texts in the same canon push in a different direction.

Ezekiel 18:20: “But the soul that sins shall die; and the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor shall the father bear the iniquity of the son.”

Deuteronomy 24:16: “The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, and the sons shall not be put to death for the fathers; everyone shall be put to death for his own sin.”

Jeremiah 31:29-30: “In those days they shall certainly not say, ‘The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge,’ but everyone shall die in his own sin.”

These are not obscure proof-texts pulled from the margins. Ezekiel is major prophetic literature. Deuteronomy is Torah. Jeremiah is prophetic canon across every Christian tradition. All three state the same principle: guilt is individual. It does not transfer across generations.

Defenders of original sin distinguish between legal guilt before human courts and spiritual solidarity before God, arguing that Ezekiel and Deuteronomy address civil justice, not the metaphysical condition inherited from Adam. Critics respond that the texts make no such distinction, they state a principle about how God judges, and they state it without qualification.

The tension between these two sets of texts is real, and both traditions acknowledge it. How you resolve it, or whether you resolve it at all, depends on which set you treat as the interpretive lens for the other.

The Councils

Augustine’s theology was forged in combat. His opponent was Pelagius, a British monk who argued that humans are born morally neutral and capable of choosing good without divine intervention. The Western church found Pelagius intolerable. Augustine’s counter, that humanity is born guilty and helpless without grace, became the institutional answer.

In 418, the Council of Carthage convened 214 bishops and issued canons against Pelagianism. Among them: that Adam was not created subject to death, that infants require baptism for the remission of sins, and that grace is necessary not only for forgiveness but for the capacity to avoid sinning at all. The canons cited Romans 5:12 using the Latin in quo omnes peccaverunt. The Western theological mind wrote this specific Latin understanding directly into its conciliar decrees.

A century later, in 529, the Second Council of Orange revisited the question. Fourteen bishops met under Caesarius of Arles and affirmed Augustine’s doctrine of sin and grace against semi-Pelagianism, the softer position that humans could at least initiate the turn toward God on their own. Orange shut that door. Many of its 25 canons used Augustine’s language word for word.

The formulation at Orange proved so durable that over a thousand years later, the Council of Trent adopted its canons with only minor variations.

Two details worth noting:

First, neither Carthage nor Orange was an ecumenical council. These were regional Western synods. They carried enormous weight in the Latin tradition, but they did not represent a universal Christian consensus.

Second, the theology they codified was substantially Augustine’s theology. One theologian’s system became the doctrinal position of the Western church, and the councils gave it formal authority.

The East

While Augustine and Pelagius fought it out in North Africa, John Chrysostom, Augustine’s exact contemporary, was reading the same passage in its original Greek and arriving somewhere else.

Chrysostom wrote, regarding Romans 5:

“For that one man should be punished on account of another does not seem to be much in accordance with reason.”

He questioned how it could follow that “from his disobedience another would become a sinner.” He acknowledged that death spread through Adam’s act. He did not conclude that guilt did.

The Eastern Orthodox tradition has never adopted Augustine’s formulation. Where the West says “original sin,” the East says “ancestral sin,” propatorikou amartimatos. The distinction is not semantic. The Greek word amartema refers to an individual act. The Eastern Fathers assigned full responsibility for the sin in the Garden to Adam and Eve alone. What passed to their descendants was death and a corrupted condition, not personal guilt for an act they did not commit.

The Eastern church does not deny the Fall or its consequences. It affirms that Adam’s transgression damaged human nature and introduced mortality. But it holds that each person bears the weight of their own sin. The inheritance from Adam is death and corruption, not culpability.

This reading predates Augustine’s mature doctrine and was widespread among the Greek Fathers. Chrysostom, the Cappadocian Fathers, and the broader Greek patristic tradition operated within this understanding for centuries. The Pelagian controversy never reached the East. Had Chrysostom been drawn into the dispute, his position would have been difficult to classify within the binary Augustine created.

The Ethiopian Church

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church represents one of the oldest continuous Christian traditions on earth, with roots predating the councils that codified Augustine’s theology. Its position aligns with the broader Eastern reading but develops it further, a surviving pre-Augustinian paradigm that never received the Western formulation because it was never in the room when the Western formulation was made.

A recent academic study examining Haimanot Abew 52:16-18 concluded that the EOTC preserves a theological tradition in which sin arises through personal moral failure rather than inherited guilt. Baptism is understood not as the removal of inherited guilt but as a sacrament of spiritual rebirth, divine adoption, and entry into communion with the Trinity.

The EOTC draws on Ezekiel 18:20, Romans 5:12-14, and Sirach 15:16 to ground its emphasis on free will, moral agency, and divine justice. Ethiopian theologians such as Abä Giyorgis and the patristic authority of Chrysostom inform the tradition’s understanding of the relationship between Adam’s act and human sinfulness.

One of those texts — Sirach — sits in the Ethiopian, Catholic, and Orthodox canons but was excluded from the Protestant Bible. The scriptural basis for the EOTC’s position on human moral agency includes a book the Western Protestant reader no longer reads.

The Reformation

Martin Luther entered the Augustinian order as a young man. He studied Augustine before he studied anyone else. When he broke from Rome, he carried Augustine’s anthropology with him, the total corruption of human nature, the bondage of the will, the inheritance of Adamic guilt from conception.

Calvin followed the same line. He defined original sin as “hereditary corruption and depravity of our nature, extending to all the parts of the soul, which first makes us obnoxious to the wrath of God.” This is Augustine’s language, nearly verbatim, filtered through a French lawyer’s precision.

The Reformers challenged Rome on authority, on sacraments, on ecclesiology, on the sale of indulgences, on the mediation of priests, on purgatory. The mainline Protestant Reformation has been described by historians as an “acute Augustinianization of Christianity.” They did not reform Augustine. They intensified him.

The 66-book Protestant canon removed the books Rome considered secondary. The Five Solas restructured the relationship between Scripture and tradition. But the doctrine of original sin — one of Rome’s most consequential theological claims — was carried across the threshold without reexamination.

The Record

Here is what the record shows.

A fourth-century North African bishop, reading Paul primarily through Latin translations, developed a specific theological claim: that the guilt of Adam’s sin transmits biologically to every human descendant. He built this partly on a rendering of Romans 5:12 that most scholars now agree does not reflect the original Greek, and partly on a broader set of scriptural texts, in Romans, the Psalms, and Genesis, that depict the human condition as damaged before any individual act of will.

Two regional Western councils codified his position, one in 418, one in 529. Neither was ecumenical. Both used Augustine’s language. The later council’s canons proved so definitive that the Council of Trent adopted them over a millennium later with minimal alteration.

The Eastern church, reading the same Scripture in its original language, at the same historical moment, arrived at a different conclusion. Death and corruption passed through Adam. Guilt did not. Each person answers for their own sin.

The Ethiopian church, one of Christianity’s oldest continuous traditions, operating from a broader scriptural canon and a pre-Augustinian theological inheritance, developed a theology of the Fall grounded in personal moral agency, free will, and the transformative power of the Incarnation rather than inherited condemnation.

The Protestant Reformers, who dismantled much of Rome’s theological and institutional apparatus, left Augustine’s doctrine of original sin untouched. Luther was an Augustinian monk.

Calvin was an Augustinian thinker.

The Reformation reformed the church’s structure. It did not reform its anthropology.

The biblical witness contains texts that support inherited spiritual solidarity and texts that insist on individual accountability. The Torah, the Prophets, and Paul all have weight in this conversation. Which set you treat as the lens for the other will determine where you land.

Every doctrine has a history. Every tradition has a genealogy. This publication exists to follow those threads wherever they lead. If you’d like to support that work, you can join the archive at: patreon.com/KingdomCode
